• Name: Red swamp crayfish
  • Common names: Red crayfish, Mudbug
  • Colour variations: Neon red crayfish, Scarlet crayfish, Ghost crayfish, White specter crayfish, etc.
  • Scientific name: Procambarus clarkii
  • Minimum tank size: 20 gallons (~90 litres)
  • Keeping: easy
  • Breeding: easy
  • Size: 10–12 cm (4–5 inches)
  • Optimal temperature: 22–27 °C (71–80 °F)
  • Optimal pH: 7.0–8.0 (6.0–9.0)
  • Optimal GH: 6–8 (3–22)
  • Optimal KH: 4–6 (2–18)
  • Optimal TDS: 150–200 (100–1000)
  • Nitrate: less than 60 ppm
  • Diet: omnivore / herbivore (as adults); omnivore / carnivore (as juveniles)
  • Temperament: very aggressive
  • Life span: up to 3 years
  • Colour forms: orange, reddish-dark, blue, yellow, white, black, but red is the main one.

Procambarus clarkii can live in almost any freshwater aquarium and is among the toughest freshwater tank inhabitants available to the hobby. This is a highly adaptable species. Its ability to grow and mature rapidly made it the dominant freshwater crayfish in the world. The only problem is that it is not suitable for planted or community tanks.

Red swamp crayfish are also highly resistant to environmental stress, including extreme temperatures, the absence of water, high salinity, and the presence of pollutants. All these qualities make it an excellent choice for beginner aquarists.

NEVER release Procambarus clarkii into the wild. Check your state laws before purchasing. This is a restricted (banned) species in some US states and European countries due to its potential to become invasive. For example, this species is listed among the 100 worst invasive species in Europe, under EU Regulation 1143/2014 regarding invasive alien species.

Can you keep it with other animals? Though it is possible for crayfish to coexist with other crayfish and fish, it is not recommended. Red swamp crayfish are naturally solitary and territorial creatures and will most often lash out at any other creature that they perceive to be invading their home. Your crayfish will live its best life when kept in a safe and solitary habitat.

Fish. Though crayfish are ultimately scavengers, they are omnivores and opportunistic eaters, which means that they can and will eat fish when given the chance. They generally will not kill a fish in one blow, but will slowly wear the fish down over a period of time through smaller attacks. Over time, the fish will become weakened due to injuries and stress. When the fish is in a much weakened state, the crayfish will prey on it. You can add small feeder fish to the tank when the intention is for them to serve as food for your crayfish. In addition, Procambarus clarkii preys on fish eggs.

Tip: If you do add fish, do not get too attached to it. Feed your crayfish daily to reduce the chances of it snatching a fish.

Snails. They are active predators of snails. For example, in Africa, Procambarus clarkii has been introduced as a biological control agent to reduce snail populations, which are intermediate hosts of schistosomiasis. Big snails potentially have a chance to survive long enough, but in general it is hard to see how they could be kept successfully in an aquarium with snails. Crayfish can eat small snails along with their shell.

Shrimp. Never keep them with shrimp; you will lose the shrimp.

Plants. This species is not plant safe. It is absolutely not possible to keep them in planted aquariums. They will eat, cut and uproot everything they can. They are lawnmowers. If you need a plant-safe crayfish, consider the Dwarf Mexican Crayfish. Adding vegetables to their diet helps, as it tends to distract them from the plants for some time.

Conclusion: Red swamp crayfish are a great, low-maintenance and easy-to-breed pet as long as the correct habitat is provided. This is a very resilient species, so beginners who make mistakes need not worry: they can adapt to new conditions. Beautiful planted tanks and Procambarus clarkii do not go together.
It is native to parts of Mexico and the United States and has established itself on all continents except Antarctica and Oceania.
Red swamp crayfish live in a variety of freshwater habitats. In the wild, they can be found in standing freshwater such as lakes, ponds, canals, irrigation ditches, rice fields, marshes, and swamps.

It is recommended to provide a tank of at least 20 gallons per adult crayfish. However, even with ample space, there is no guarantee that the crayfish will not act in a territorial manner, attacking and even eating their tank mates. Procambarus clarkii will be perfectly happy to be the only pet in the tank.

Important: Crayfish are excellent escape artists. Therefore, hide or protect all cables in any tank.

Procambarus clarkii is extremely tolerant of poor water quality. Although it can tolerate and reproduce in a wide range of aquatic environments, caring for your crayfish still requires some specific knowledge and skills.

Substrate. Procambarus clarkii will dig a lot, so a layer of a few cm of aquarium soil, sand or fine gravel (about 5–8 cm) is the best choice. This helps your crayfish feel safe and stress-free. Aquascaping does not work with crayfish: they will push, drag, dig and rearrange everything in the tank.

Plants. Floating, cheap and fast-growing live plants are a great choice for crayfish tanks as they can serve as natural food. Live plants also help keep the tank clean and provide safety and protection, which can reduce territorial and aggressive behaviour. Artificial plants are a lower-maintenance option that is perfectly fine; they still provide functional hiding places.

Decorations and hiding places. Provide lots of places to hide, or they will burrow and dig even more often than usual. Crayfish naturally like to have shelter and safety, be it from rocks, driftwood or plants.

Filtration. A sponge filter is a bad idea with these crayfish (though still possible), because they like to chip and chew on it. With time, Procambarus clarkii will simply tear the sponge apart. Do not put them in an uncycled tank. Although they are quite hardy and can potentially survive even during cycling, you do not want to take your chances.

Bubbler. If the aquascape does not allow your crayfish to get to the surface, add a bubbler, as they need oxygenated water. Although Procambarus clarkii can live in swamps, they cannot swim far up for oxygen, so they crawl out onto land from time to time.

Tolerance:

  • Adult red swamp crayfish can live in salinity <15%. Tolerance to salinity is directly proportional to crayfish size. Newly hatched young die at 15 parts per thousand (ppt), and juveniles die at 30 ppt after one week.
  • Temperature range of 8–33 °C (46–91 °F).
  • Although this crayfish is an aquatic species, it is highly resistant to air exposure and can survive for several days outside the water (under humid conditions).
  • They can ingest and eventually store large amounts of heavy metals in their tissues.
  • They are very tolerant of copper. Procambarus clarkii has physiological mechanisms to regulate copper levels, which enable it to cope with exposure to higher levels of copper in its environment without tissue bioaccumulation.

When you get your crayfish, it should come in a plastic bag or container of water. Do not put it directly in the tank: changing the water temperature too quickly can shock the crayfish. Regardless of their hardiness, it is better to acclimate them.

Molting. Crayfish must molt, or shed their hard exoskeleton, to increase in size. Molting interval and growth rate are affected by water temperature, population density, water quality, and food quality and quantity. Depending on age and water temperature, molt intervals range from 4 to 30 days. For example, baby crayfish molt every few days, while juvenile crayfish may molt every 7–10 days.

The molting process is controlled by environmental and endocrine hormones, which are located in the eyestalks. Like all crustaceans, Procambarus clarkii becomes very lethargic for a few days beforehand and does not eat as much. Cloudy eyes are a sign that it is going to molt.

After molting, the metabolic demand for calcium (to harden the shell) is particularly great. Crayfish use calcium to produce a new and healthy shell. These nutrients are necessary in abundance, especially following molting.

Ideal water parameters: pH 7–8, temperature 22–27 °C, GH 6–8, KH 4–6. Test your water frequently to ensure the water is hard and the pH is on the alkaline side; otherwise your crayfish can have trouble molting.

Procambarus clarkii is a generalist omnivore and a natural scavenger. As a nocturnal animal, it most actively seeks food in the early morning and just before dark.

In their natural habitat, crayfish feed on plants, algae, animal detritus, macrophytes, and dead and live animals such as molluscs, insects, annelids, nematodes, platyhelminths, tadpoles, fingerlings, fish, snails, etc.

Crayfish do not exhibit a preference for any animal prey. According to multiple studies, pre-adults and adults tend to be more herbivorous, whereas juveniles tend to be more predatory. Juveniles cannot be classified as true detritivores or herbivores since they rely on animal prey for their rapid growth. For example, the diet composition is:

JuvenileAdult
Animal matter44%20%
Detritus29%41%
Plants27%39%

However, when food resources are limited, crayfish lose much of their selectivity and will consume almost any plant or animal food items.

Make sure the diet of your crayfish is rich in nutrients, especially calcium and iodine. If you are unsure of the nutrient makeup of the food you are feeding, supplement the diet with store-bought crustacean pellets, which are formulated to contain the full spectrum of nutrients. Boiled lettuce, cabbage, zucchini, carrots, etc. are a popular choice.

It is best to feed in the early morning or at dusk, when the crayfish is likely to be most active.

Tip: Once your crayfish has had a few hours of food present at its peak feeding time, remove any unused food to avoid the growth of unwanted bacteria in the tank.

Tip #2: Colour-enhancing foods such as Hikari Shrimp Cuisine, Hikari Micro Wafers and Hikari Tropical Crab Cuisine can be a good option to maintain or improve the colouration of your crayfish.

Procambarus clarkii can make great aquarium pets if you understand their natural tendencies and behaviours and care for them accordingly.

This species is nocturnal, although some individuals do not mind being active even during the day. They have two movement patterns: one or more short peaks of intense locomotion ("wandering" phases) alternating with periods of scarce mobility, with slow speeds or no movement ("stationary" phases).

They are very aggressive and tend to fight almost all the time. Procambarus clarkii is a solitary and territorial creature. They will pinch and claw when they feel threatened. A large tank is crucial if you try to keep multiple crayfish together.

It is possible to hold your crayfish on a flat palm when they are calm, but keep in mind that they can defend themselves. Tip: If you are new to handling crayfish or have children handling the animals, consider scooping the crayfish up into a plastic cup when handling must occur.

Like many crayfish species, Procambarus clarkii is an efficient digger. In the absence of shelter, both males and females begin burrowing rapidly. In the wild, burrows are used as a refuge to avoid predation, dehydration and environmental stress, as well as for nesting. According to observations, the average length of excavated tunnels ranges from 20–80 cm.

Interesting fact: Despite the great importance of these shelters, they seem not to return to previously occupied burrows at the end of their foraging excursions, despite the time and energy expended to excavate them.

Sexually mature Procambarus clarkii exhibit distinct characteristics, including darker coloration, enlarged claws, and hardened sexual structures. Mature males develop prominent hooks (the genital pores) at the base of the third and fourth pair of pereiopods (walking legs), whereas in females the first pair of abdominal appendages has no modification.

Mating. It may sometimes be difficult to determine whether crayfish are mating or simply fighting. When the male approaches the female, she will usually react aggressively at first. After sex recognition, the male courts the female through a specific sequence of movements followed by copulation. The male flips the female over and deposits the spermatophore in a protective receptacle in the female.

According to studies, the role of the female is not always passive. If a female is in a high sexual state and a male is inactive, on a few occasions the female may attempt to move even underneath the male. Mating usually occurs in open water before females start to burrow.

The smallest ovigerous female captured was 39.5 mm. Males usually reach maturity at 25–40 mm in length.

Interesting fact: Strength plays no role in mating. Even when the female is bigger and stronger than the male, she will let him "defeat" her and flip her over. Studies show that if females are not ready to mate, they will always escape, even when the males are bigger and stronger.

Breeding. Depending on environmental conditions, after mating the female shelters in a burrow and starts oviposition. In the wild this process may occur in open water, but this is very uncommon.

The number of eggs varies with female size and water temperature. A 10 cm female may produce up to 500–900 eggs, while smaller females may produce around 100–200. At low temperatures (13 °C), even large females produce only 30–40 eggs (ten times fewer).

Eggs have 6 stages of development. Egg diameter increases from 0.3 mm in stage 2 to up to 1.6 mm in stage 6. Developing eggs increase in size and change from a light colour to dark as they mature.

Once laid, eggs hatch in as little as 3 weeks at 21–24 °C (70–75 °F) and in 4 to 5 months at 12–15.6 °C (53–60 °F). Growth is inhibited at temperatures below 12 °C.

Interesting fact: Procambarus clarkii can reproduce in slightly brackish water (5 g/L salinity).

Rearing the young. Separate the gravid female from other crayfish, the sooner the better. A second tank is needed, but it does not need to be big because at that stage females do not move much and tend to hide in their shelter (or burrow) all the time.

Newly hatched crayfish remain attached to the pleopods (swimmerets) on the female's abdomen through several molts, or about 30–35 days. Hatchlings remain with the female for several weeks after their second molt, although they are no longer attached to the swimmerets.

Once the young leave the mother's tail, put her back into the main tank and leave the young in the new tank, to prevent any aggression from her.

Their complete separation from the mother is followed by 2 to 3 weeks of voracious eating. At this stage they require a lot of protein, and in the absence of food they can quickly start cannibalizing. Therefore, provide plenty of hiding places with rocks and loose debris so the young can hide from each other.

Under ideal conditions of 22–30 °C (75–86 °F), crayfish can mature in 3 months. A minimum of 11 molts is necessary for hatchlings to grow to sexual maturity.

In general, this species has a dark red body (carapace). In the aquarium trade, however, different colour variations can be found:

  • Orange (Neon red crayfish)
  • Reddish dark (Scarlet crayfish)
  • Blue (Ghost crayfish)
  • Yellow (Orange ghost or Fireball crayfish)
  • White (White specter crayfish)
  • Black varieties

One of the unique things about them is that they have a hook on the claws. In addition, unlike other crayfish species, Procambarus clarkii does not have an areola on the back (unlike its cousin Procambarus alleni, the Blue crayfish).

Juveniles are usually light green with a narrow dark band on either side of the abdomen and a broader lighter band along the dorsal surface.

Fully grown Procambarus clarkii can reach 3.5–12 cm (2.2 to 4.7 inches) in length. There are reports that in the wild some individuals can measure up to 15 cm (6 inches). Life span does not exceed 3 years but can reach 5 years in higher latitudes.
